title: When the Killer Is a Recycler

scenes.visual: Title card 'When the Killer Is a Recycler' fades in over a blue ocean surface seen from the side. Same COLOUR MAP as the first film: nitrogen = GREEN dots; phosphorus = ORANGE dots; bacteria = small PURPLE rods; viruses = small RED nearly round particles (never cubes); algae = round GREEN-OLIVE cells; host-to-pathogen harm = DARK GREY one-way arrow. GREY PADLOCK icon for locked matter, which springs open when matter is released; the tracker bar 'locked' to 'usable' runs along the bottom. Labelled blocks and cartoons only, never molecular structures. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Cream background, 16:9.

scenes.tts: Some pathogens kill the very cells they infect, and viruses often do. That arrow from the first film ran one way, from host to pathogen. But when a virus kills a cell, where does that cell's matter go?
scenes.visual: A quick recap strip: the grapevine with its DARK GREY one-way arrow from the first film shrinks into the top-left corner. A question mark appears beside it, then slides down into the ocean below.
scenes.narration: Some pathogens kill the very cells they infect, and viruses often do. That arrow from the first film ran one way, from host to pathogen. But when a virus kills a cell, where does that cell's matter go?

scenes.tts: Picture a virus bursting a cell in the ocean. A moment ago, that cell held nitrogen. Where is that nitrogen now?
scenes.visual: Zoom into seawater. One round GREEN-OLIVE cell, its inside dotted with GREEN nitrogen dots under a GREY PADLOCK. A RED nearly round virus drifts toward it. Freeze just before contact; a label asks 'where does the nitrogen go?'
scenes.narration: Picture a virus bursting a cell in the ocean. A moment ago, that cell held nitrogen. Where is that nitrogen now?

scenes.tts: Ocean water holds enormous numbers of viruses. A virus that infects bacteria is called a bacteriophage, or phage for short. Other ocean viruses infect algae.
scenes.visual: Pull back to show many RED virus particles among PURPLE rods and GREEN-OLIVE algae cells, labelled 'schematic'. A RED particle sits on a PURPLE rod with the label 'bacteriophage (phage): infects bacteria'. Another RED particle sits on an algae cell, labelled 'other viruses: infect algae'.
scenes.narration: Ocean water holds enormous numbers of viruses. A virus that infects bacteria is called a bacteriophage, or phage for short. Other ocean viruses infect algae.

scenes.tts: Researchers built a lab model ecosystem. It was a flask of seawater with an ocean alga called Fay-oh-sis-tis. Then they added a virus that infects it.
scenes.caption: Researchers built a lab model ecosystem. It was a flask of seawater with an ocean alga called Phaeocystis. Then they added a virus that infects it.
scenes.visual: A lab flask fills with seawater; GREEN-OLIVE cells labelled 'Phaeocystis' float inside. A dropper adds RED nearly round virus particles. Label on the flask: 'lab model ecosystem'.
scenes.narration: Researchers built a lab model ecosystem. It was a flask of seawater with an ocean alga called Phaeocystis. Then they added a virus that infects it.

scenes.tts: The viruses infected the algae. Then the cells burst, spilling much of what was inside them into the water. The algae were dead. Was their nitrogen gone too?
scenes.visual: Close-up inside the flask: RED particles stick to an alga. The cell bursts into GREEN-OLIVE fragments and tan debris. The GREY PADLOCK floats among the debris, still closed.
scenes.narration: The viruses infected the algae. Then the cells burst, spilling much of what was inside them into the water. The algae were dead. Was their nitrogen gone too?

scenes.tts: No. Bacteria swarmed the remains and broke them down. The water gained nitrogen and phosphorus, in forms other living things could use. Algae and bacteria can take them up.
scenes.visual: PURPLE rods swarm the tan debris and nibble it smaller. GREEN nitrogen dots and ORANGE phosphorus dots spread through the water. The padlock springs open and the tracker marker slides to 'usable'. Surviving algae cells and PURPLE rods absorb some GREEN and ORANGE dots. No numbers on screen.
scenes.narration: No. Bacteria swarmed the remains and broke them down. The water gained nitrogen and phosphorus, in forms other living things could use. Algae and bacteria can take them up.

scenes.tts: So the nitrogen was not destroyed. The virus killed the cell, but much of the cell's matter went back into the water. A killer can also be part of a recycling chain. Virus, then bacteria, then other living things: each step moves matter on.
scenes.visual: Recap loop in three small frames joined by arrows: 'virus infects the alga', 'cell bursts, bacteria break down remains', 'nitrogen and phosphorus in the water: other living things use them'. The DARK GREY arrow from cell to virus is followed by GREEN and ORANGE arrows fanning out to other cells.
scenes.narration: So the nitrogen was not destroyed. The virus killed the cell, but much of the cell's matter went back into the water. A killer can also be part of a recycling chain. Virus, then bacteria, then other living things: each step moves matter on.

scenes.tts: Now zoom out to a whole landscape, the Serengeti in East Africa. Rinderpest is a virus disease of cattle and of wild grazing animals, such as wildebeest.
scenes.visual: The flask shrinks to a dot and the view pulls back to a savanna map labelled 'Serengeti, East Africa'. Cartoon cattle and a herd of wildebeest graze on golden grass; a RED virus icon labelled 'rinderpest' hovers over both.
scenes.narration: Now zoom out to a whole landscape, the Serengeti in East Africa. Rinderpest is a virus disease of cattle and of wild grazing animals, such as wildebeest.

scenes.tts: In the nineteen sixties, vaccinating cattle wiped rinderpest out of the Serengeti. The virus was gone. What happened to the land?
scenes.caption: In the 1960s, vaccinating cattle wiped rinderpest out of the Serengeti. The virus was gone. What happened to the land?
scenes.visual: On-screen year tag '1960s'. A syringe icon taps each cow; the RED rinderpest icon cracks and fades. A four-link chain appears across the top, all links still dark: 'rinderpest gone', '?', '?', '?'.
scenes.narration: In the 1960s, vaccinating cattle wiped rinderpest out of the Serengeti. The virus was gone. What happened to the land?

scenes.tts: Here is a question to try. With rinderpest gone, will the Serengeti end up with more trees, or with fewer trees?
scenes.visual: Hold on the savanna with a few scattered young trees. Two answer cards slide in: 'more trees' and 'fewer trees'. They pulse gently.
scenes.narration: Here is a question to try. With rinderpest gone, will the Serengeti end up with more trees, or with fewer trees?

scenes.visual: Hold on the two answer cards. A small 5-second countdown ring empties in the corner.

scenes.tts: More trees. Researchers traced the chain using decades of records and computer models. First, wildebeest numbers rose. More wildebeest ate more grass.
scenes.visual: The card 'more trees' lights up. The second chain link lights: the wildebeest herd grows across the map (labelled 'schematic'). The third link lights: the golden grass is grazed short.
scenes.narration: More trees. Researchers traced the chain using decades of records and computer models. First, wildebeest numbers rose. More wildebeest ate more grass.

scenes.tts: Less dry grass meant less fuel for fires. Fewer fires burned, so more young trees survived. Their analysis supported this chain, from the loss of one virus to more trees.
scenes.visual: Fourth link lights: small fire icons shrink and fewer appear. Young trees sprout and survive across the map, which turns greener (labelled 'schematic'). The full lit chain reads: 'rinderpest gone, more wildebeest, more grass eaten, fewer fires, more trees'.
scenes.narration: Less dry grass meant less fuel for fires. Fewer fires burned, so more young trees survived. Their analysis supported this chain, from the loss of one virus to more trees.

scenes.tts: Two scales, two lessons. In the flask, matter from the dead cells went back into the water for other living things. On the savanna, losing one virus changed which populations grew. Viruses that burst cells can recycle matter. Pathogens can reshape ecosystems.
scenes.visual: Split screen with no shared arrow. Left: the flask with GREEN and ORANGE dots being taken up, labelled 'matter moves on'. Right: the greener savanna with its lit chain, labelled 'populations change'. A caption bar under both reads 'recycle and reshape'.
scenes.narration: Two scales, two lessons. In the flask, matter from the dead cells went back into the water for other living things. On the savanna, losing one virus changed which populations grew. Viruses that burst cells can recycle matter. Pathogens can reshape ecosystems.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line on screen: 'Viruses that burst cells can recycle matter; pathogens can reshape ecosystems.'
